¶
'''whereabout''' (hwãr′a-bout″), ''n.'' [< ''whereabout'', ''adv.''] The place where one is; one’s present place.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou . . . firm-set earth,
Hear not my steps, which way they walk, for fear
Thy very stones prate of my ''whereabout.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, ii. 1. 58.}}
<poem>From a rifted crag or ivy tod . . .
Thou giv’st for pastime’s sake, by shriek or shout,
A puzzling notice of thy ''whereabout.''</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Evening Voluntaries, vii.}}}}

'''whereabouts''' (hwãr′a-bouts′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' [< ''whereabout'' + adv. gen. ''-s''.] Same as ''whereabout''.

'''whereabouts''' (hwãr′a-bouts″), ''n.'' [< ''whereabouts'', ''adv.''] The place where one or where anything is; location; locality.
{{smaller block|I feel as if it were scarcely discreet to indicate the ''whereabouts'' of the château of the obliging young man I had met on the way from Nîmes; I must content myself with saying that it nestled in an enchanting valley.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 171.}}}}

'''whereagainst''' (hwãr′a-genst′), ''conj.'' [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''against''.] Against which.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let me twine
Mine arms about that body, ''where against''
My grained ash an hundred times hath broke.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iv. 5. 113.}}}}

'''whereas''' (hwãr-az′), ''conj.'' [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''as''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' The thing being so that; considering that things are so: implying an admission of facts,
readings.c1s2:
sometimes followed by a different statement, and sometimes by inference or something consequent, as in the preamble to a law or a resolution.

{{smaller block|''Whereas'', A consistent and faithful adherence to the principles of administrative reform . . . is absolutely essential to the vitality and success of the . . . party; . . .
Resolved, That . . . the character, record, and associations of its candidates . . . should be such as to warrant entire confidence.
{{right|Quoted in ''Appleton’s Annual Cyc.'', 1884, p. 767.}}}}
'''2.''' While on the contrary; the fact or case really being that; when in fact.
{{smaller block|''Whereas'', before, our forefathers had no other books but the score and the tally, thou hast caused printing to be used.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iv. 7. 37.}}
If I were wise only to mine own ends, I would certainly take such a subject as of it self might catch applause, ''whereas'' this hath all the disadvantages on the contrary.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, ii., Pref.}}}}
'''3†.''' Where.
{{smaller block|<poem>Soone he came ''where-as'' the Titanesse
Was striving with faire Cynthia for her seat.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VII. vi. 17.}}
<poem>He, spying her, bounced in, ''whereas'' he stood.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Passionate Pilgrim, l. 83.}}}}

'''whereat''' (hwãr-at′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''at''.] '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' At what? as, ''whereat'' are you offended? ''Johnson.''

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' At which.
{{smaller block|<poem>Even at this word she hears a merry horn,
''Whereat'' she leaps that was but late forlorn.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 1026.}}
<poem>He now prepared
To speak; ''whereat'' their doubled ranks they bend
From wing to wing, and half inclose him round.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 616.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Whereinsoever'' ye shall perceive yourselves to have offended, . . . there to bewail your own sinfulness.
{{right|''Book of Common Prayer'', Communion office, Exhortation.}}}}

'''whereinto''' (hwãr-in′tö or -in-tö′), ''adv.'' [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''into.''] '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' Into what?

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' Into which.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where’s that palace ''whereinto'' foul things
Sometimes intrude not? ''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3. 137.</poem>
I watched my opportunitie to get a shore in their Boat, ''whereinto'' the darke night I secretly got.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 212.}}}}

'''wheremid†''', ''conj.'' [< ME. ''whermid'', ''hwermid'', ''wermid'' (= D. ''waarmede'' = G. ''womit'' = Sw. ''hvarmed'' = Dan. ''hvormed''); < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''mid''<sup>2</sup>.] Wherewith.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nothing he ne founde in al the niȝte
''Wer-mide'' his honger aquenche miȝtte.</poem>
{{right|''Rel. Antiq.'', II. 274.}}
Thet is the dyeules peni ''huermide'' he bayth [buyeth].
{{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 23.}}}}

'''whereness''' (hwãr′nes), ''n.'' [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness.''] The state or property of having place or position; ubication.
{{smaller block|A point hath no dimensions, but only a ''whereness'', and is next to nothing. ''N. Grew'', Cosmologia Sacra.
Ubication or ''whereness''. ''Whewell.''}}

'''whereof''' (hwãr-ov′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.'' [< ME. ''wher of'', ''wharof'', ''worof'', ''hvarof'' (= Sw. ''hvaraf'' = Dan. ''hvoraf''), < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''of.''] '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' Of what? from what?
{{smaller block|<poem>''Quarof'' ard thou so ferd?
Hit is a litil synne.</poem>
{{right|''MS. Cantab.'' Ff. v. 48. f. 82. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}

¶
'''whereso''' (hwãr′sō), ''conj.'' [< ME. ''whereso;'' < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''so''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. AS. ''swā hwǣr swā.''] Wheresoever.
{{smaller block|<poem>Of ble as the brere flour ''where-so'' the bare scheweed [showed]
Ful clene watz the countenaunce of her [their] cler yȝen.</poem>
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 790.}}
<poem>Furnished with deadly instruments she went
Of every sort, to wound ''whereso'' she meant.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton,'' Barons’ Wars, ii. 5.}}}}

'''wheresoe’er''' (hwãr-sọ̄-ãr′), ''conj.'' A contracted form of ''wheresoever.''

'''wheresoever''' (hwãr-sọ̄-ev′ėr), ''conj.'' [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''so''<sup>1</sup> + ''ever.''] '''1.''' In what place soever; in whatever place.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wheresoever'' I am sung or told
In aftertime, this also shall be known.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson,'' Passing of Arthur.}}}}
'''2†.''' Whencesoever.
{{smaller block|This is some minx’s token, and I must take out the work? . . . ''Wheresoever'' you had it, I’ll take out no work on ’t.
{{right|''Shak.,'' Othello, iv. 1. 160.}}}}
'''3.''' Whithersoever; to what place soever.
{{smaller block|<poem>The noise pursues me ''wheresoe’er'' I go.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden,'' Aurengzebe, v. 1.}}}}

'''wherethorough†''' (hwãr-thur′ō), ''conj.'' [< ME. ''wherthur, hwarthuruh, huerthurh;'' < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''thorough'' (see ''thorough'' and ''through''<sup>1</sup>).] Same as ''wherethrough.''

'''wherethrough''' (hwãr-thrö′), ''conj.'' [Also ''wherethro’;'' < ME. ''wherthrough;'' < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''through''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''wherethorough.''] Through which, in any sense of the word ''through.''

{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 171.}}}}

Mine arms about that body, ''where against''

{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iv. 5. 113.}}}}

'''whereas''' (hwãr-az′), ''conj.''   [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''as''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' The thing being so that; considering that things are so: implying an admission of facts, sometimes followed by a different statement, and sometimes by inference or something consequent, as in the preamble to a law or a resolution.

{{smaller block|''Whereas'', A consistent and faithful adherence to the principles of administrative reform . . . is absolutely essential to the vitality and success of the . . . party; . . .
Resolved, That . . . the character, record, and associations of its candidates . . . should be such as to warrant entire confidence.
{{right|Quoted in ''Appleton’s Annual Cyc.'', 1884, p. 767.}}}}
'''2.''' While on the contrary; the fact or case really being that; when in fact.
{{smaller block|''Whereas'', before, our forefathers had no other books but the score and the tally, thou hast caused printing to be used.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iv. 7. 37.}}}}
{{smaller block|If I were wise only to mine own ends, I would certainly take such a subject as of it self might catch applause, ''whereas'' this hath all the disadvantages on the contrary.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, ii., Pref.}}}}
'''3†.''' Where.
{{smaller block|<poem>Soone he came ''where-as'' the Titanesse
Was striving with faire Cynthia for her seat.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VII. vi. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He, spying her, bounced in, ''whereas'' he stood.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Passionate Pilgrim, l. 83.}}}}

'''whereat''' (hwãr-at′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''at''.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' At what? as, ''whereat'' are you offended?   ''Johnson.''

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' At which.
{{smaller block|<poem>Even at this word she hears a merry horn,
''Whereat'' she leaps that was but late forlorn.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 1026.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He now prepared
To speak; ''whereat'' their doubled ranks they bend
From wing to wing, and half inclose him round.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 616.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whereat'' erewhile I wept, I laugh. {{right|''Greene'', Song.}}}}

'''whereby''' (hwãr-bī′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wharbi'' (= D. ''waarbij'' = G. ''wobei''); < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''by''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' By what? how? why?
{{smaller block|''Wharbi'' seistow [sayest thou] so?
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2256.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whereby'' shall I know this? {{right|Luke i. 18.}}}}

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' By which, in any sense of the word ''by.''
{{smaller block|<poem>You take my life
When you do take the means ''whereby'' I live.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iv. 1. 377.}}}}
{{smaller block|But this word Werowance, which we call and construe for a King, is a common word, ''whereby'' they call all commanders. {{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 143.}}}}
{{smaller block|The mind . . . has a power to abstract its ideas, and so they become essences, general essences, ''whereby'' the sorts of things are distinguished.
{{right|''Locke'', Human Understanding, III. viii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Fear
Stared in her eyes, and chalk’d her face, and wing’d
Her transit to the throne, ''whereby'' she fell
Delivering seal’d dispatches.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}}

'''where’er''' (hwãr-ãr′), ''adv.'' A contracted form of ''wherever.''

'''wherefore''' (hwãr′fōr), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [Early mod. E. ''wherfore''; < ME. ''wherfore'', ''wherfor'', ''hwarfore'' (= D. ''waarvoor'' = G. ''wofür'' = Sw. ''hvarför'' = Dan. ''hvorfor''); < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''fore''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' For what reason, thing, or purpose? what for? why?
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wherefore'' was I born?
If that my cousin king be King of England,
It must be granted I am Duke of Lancaster.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 3. 122.}}}}

{{smaller block|If Princes need no palliations, as he tells his Son, ''wherefore'' is it that he himself hath so oft’n us’d them?
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xxvii.}}}}

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' For which cause or reason; in consequence of which; consequently.
{{smaller block|<poem>Dedes therof mak the cause ther-on be,
Off the lordes yifte the encheson may se,
''Wher-for'' he it yaf, and for wat reason.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 558.}}}}
{{smaller block|He pardoneth and absolveth all those who truly repent. . . . ''Wherefore'' let us beseech him to grant us true repentance.
{{right|''Book of Common Prayer'', Absolution.}}}}
{{smaller block|The night was as troublesome to him as the day; ''wherefore'', instead of sleeping, he spent it in sighs and tears.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}}

'''To do wherefore†''', {{smaller|to make a return; give or furnish an equivalent.}}
{{smaller block|No wollemongere, ne no man, ne may habbe no stal in the heye-stret of Wynchestre bote he ''do war-fore''.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 353.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Therefore'', ''Wherefore'', ''Accordingly'', etc. See ''therefore''.}}

'''wherefore''' (hwãr′fōr), ''n.''   [< ''wherefore'', ''adv.'']   The reason or cause. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Dispute learnedly the whys and ''wherefores''.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Rule a Wife, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The way and the ''wherefore'' of it all
Who knoweth?</poem>
{{right|''Jean Ingelow.''}}}}

'''wherefrom''' (hwãr-from′), ''conj.''   [= Sw. ''hvarifrån'' = Dan. ''hvorfra''; as ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''from''.]   From which; whence.
{{smaller block|<poem>In each a squared lawn, ''wherefrom''
The golden gorge of dragons spouted forth
A flood of fountain-foam.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Palace of Art.}}}}
{{smaller block|A larger surface ''wherefrom'' material can be washed into the lagoon.
{{right|''Nature'', XLII. 148.}}}}

'''wherehence†''', ''conj.''   [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''hence''.]   Whence. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He had lived two years at Campostella, . . . ''wherehence'' he then came.
{{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 20.}}}}

'''wherein''' (hwãr-in′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wherin'', ''hverinne'' (= D. ''waarin'' = G. ''worin'' = Sw. ''hvari'' = Dan. ''hvori''), wherein; < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''in''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' In what? in what thing, time, respect, etc.?
{{smaller block|But ye say, ''Wherein'' have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.
{{right|Mal. iii. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|How looked he? ''Wherein'' [that is, in what clothes] went he?
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 2. 234.}}}}

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' '''1.''' In or within which or what; in which thing, time, respect, etc.
{{smaller block|This zenne [sin] is the dyeules panne of helle, ''huerinne'' he maketh his friinges [fryings].
{{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You naked trees, whose shady leaves are lost,
''Wherein'' the byrds were wont to build their bowre.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., January.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Alfantica is also a place of note, because it is invironed with a great wall, ''wherein'' lye the goods of all the Merchants securely guarded.
{{right|''Capt. John Smith'', True Travels, I. 45.}}}}
{{smaller block|Milton seems to have known perfectly well ''wherein'' his strength lay.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 315.}}}}
'''2.''' In that in which; in whatever.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wherein'' it doth impair the seeing sense,
It pays the hearing double recompense.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 2. 180.}}}}

'''whereinsoever''' (hwãr-in′sō-ev′ėr), ''conj.'' In whatever place, point, or respect.

{{smaller block|''Whereinsoever'' ye shall perceive yourselves to have offended, . . . there to bewail your own sinfulness.
{{right|''Book of Common Prayer'', Communion office, Exhortation.}}}}

'''whereinto''' (hwãr-in′tö or -in-tö′), ''adv.''   [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''into.'']   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' Into what?

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' Into which.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where’s that palace ''whereinto'' foul things
Sometimes intrude not? ''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3. 137.</poem>
I watched my opportunitie to get a shore in their Boat, ''whereinto'' the darke night I secretly got.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 212.}}}}

'''wheremid†''', ''conj.''   [< ME. ''whermid'', ''hwermid'', ''wermid'' (= D. ''waarmede'' = G. ''womit'' = Sw. ''hvarmed'' = Dan. ''hvormed''); < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''mid''<sup>2</sup>.]   Wherewith.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nothing he ne founde in al the niȝte
''Wer-mide'' his honger aquenche miȝtte.</poem>
{{right|''Rel. Antiq.'', II. 274.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thet is the dyeules peni ''huermide'' he bayth [buyeth].
{{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 23.}}}}

'''whereness''' (hwãr′nes), ''n.''   [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness.'']   The state or property of having place or position; ubication.
{{smaller block|A point hath no dimensions, but only a ''whereness'', and is next to nothing. ''N. Grew'', Cosmologia Sacra.
Ubication or ''whereness''.
{{right|''Whewell.''}}}}

'''whereof''' (hwãr-ov′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wher of'', ''wharof'', ''worof'', ''hvarof'' (= Sw. ''hvaraf'' = Dan. ''hvoraf''), < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''of.'']   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' Of what? from what?
{{smaller block|<poem>''Quarof'' ard thou so ferd?
Hit is a litil synne.</poem>
{{right|''MS. Cantab.'' Ff. v. 48. f. 82. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|Now, gods that we adore, ''whereof'' comes this?
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4. 312.}}}}

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' Of which; of whom.

<poem>For lente neuere was lyf, but lyflode [means of livelihood] were shapen,
''Wher-of'' or wherfore or where-by to lybbe.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xiv. 40.}}}}

{{smaller block|The days are made on a loom ''whereof'' the warp and woof are past and future time.
{{right|''Emerson'', Works and Days.}}}}

'''whereon''' (hwãr-on′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wheron'', ''hveran'' (= D. ''waaraan'' = G. ''woran''); < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''on''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' On what? on whom?

<poem>''Queen. Whereon'' do you look?
''Ham.'' On him, on him! {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 4. 124.}}</poem>

'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' On which.

<poem>O fair foundation laid ''whereon'' to build
Their ruin! {{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 521.}}</poem>

<poem>How He who bore in Heav’n the second name
Had not on earth ''whereon'' to lay His head.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Burns'', Cottar’s Saturday Night.}}}}

'''whereout''' (hwãr-out′), ''conj.''   [= D. ''waaruit;'' as ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''out''.]   Out of which.

<poem>That I may give the local wound a name
And make distinct the very breach ''whereout''
Hector’s great spirit flew.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., iv. 5. 245.}}}}

{{smaller block|The cleft ''whereout'' the lightning breaketh. {{right|''Holland.''}}}}

'''whereover''' (hwãr-ō′vėr), ''conj.'' Over which. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|A great gulf . . . ''whereover'' neither Dives nor Abraham, nor yet Moses himself, can pass.
{{right|''T. Parker'', On the Death of Daniel Webster, p. 7.}}}}

'''whereso''' (hwãr′sō), ''conj.''   [< ME. ''whereso;'' < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''so''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. AS. ''swā hwǣr swā.'']   Wheresoever.
{{smaller block|<poem>Of ble as the brere flour ''where-so'' the bare scheweed [showed]
Ful clene watz the countenaunce of her [their] cler yȝen.</poem>
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 790.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Furnished with deadly instruments she went

{{right|''Drayton,'' Barons’ Wars, ii. 5.}}}}

'''wheresoe’er''' (hwãr-sọ̄-ãr′), ''conj.'' A contracted form of ''wheresoever.''

'''wheresoever''' (hwãr-sọ̄-ev′ėr), ''conj.''   [< ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''so''<sup>1</sup> + ''ever.'']   '''1.''' In what place soever; in whatever place.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wheresoever'' I am sung or told
In aftertime, this also shall be known.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson,'' Passing of Arthur.}}}}
'''2†.''' Whencesoever.
{{smaller block|This is some minx’s token, and I must take out the work? . . . ''Wheresoever'' you had it, I’ll take out no work on ’t.
{{right|''Shak.,'' Othello, iv. 1. 160.}}}}
'''3.''' Whithersoever; to what place soever.
{{smaller block|<poem>The noise pursues me ''wheresoe’er'' I go.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden,'' Aurengzebe, v. 1.}}}}

'''wherethorough†''' (hwãr-thur′ō), ''conj.''   [< ME. ''wherthur, hwarthuruh, huerthurh;'' < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''thorough'' (see ''thorough'' and ''through''<sup>1</sup>).]   Same as ''wherethrough.''

'''wherethrough''' (hwãr-thrö′), ''conj.''   [Also ''wherethro’;'' < ME. ''wherthrough;'' < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''through''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''wherethorough.'']   Through which, in any sense of the word ''through.''

{{smaller block|<poem>He . . . hath beaute, ''wher-through'' he is
Worthy of love to have the blis.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 3733.}}}}
{{smaller block|A way without impediment, . . . ''wherethrough'' all the people went.
{{right|Wisdom xix. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|There is no weakness left in me ''wherethrough'' I may look back.
{{right|''Scott.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet all experience is an arch ''wherethro’''
Gleams that untravell’d world, whose margin fades
For ever and for ever when I move.</poem>

'''whereto''' (hwãr-tö′), ''adv.'' and ''conj.''   [< ME. ''hwarto, hvarto, war to, hwerto'' (= D. ''waartoe'' = G. ''wozu''); < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''to''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''interrog. adv.'' To what place, point, end, etc.?
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wherto'' bounet ye to batell in your bright geire,
Whethur worship to wyn, or willfully shame?</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 6565.}}}}
{{smaller block|Lysander, ''whereto'' tends all this?
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 2. 256.}}}}
'''II.''' ''rel. conj.'' To which; to whom; whither.
{{smaller block|They may, by his direction, be employed principally in suche profession ''whereto'' their nature doth most conforme.
{{right|''Booke of Precedence'' (E. E. T. S., extra ser.), i. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|Purposing to be of that Religion ''whereto'' they should addict themselves.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 46.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>This battle in the west,
''Whereto'' we move.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Passing of Arthur.}}}}

'''whereunder''' (hwãr-un′dėr), ''conj.''   [< ME. ''huer-onder'' (= D. ''waaronder'' = G. ''worunter'' = Sw. ''hvarunder'' = Dan. ''hvorunder''); < ''where''<sup>1</sup> + ''under''.]   Under which.
{{smaller block|The wild-grape vines . . . ''whereunder'' we had slept.
